opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that it's really the same story we've been seeing for a long time, just showing up in a new place. Going back to when I first started thinking about scaling, around 2017 or so, the picture I had in my head was what I sometimes call the "big blob of compute" hypothesis. The idea is that a lot of the cleverness people put into specific techniques doesn't matter that much. What matters is a handful of things: how much raw compute you have, how much data, the quality and distribution of that data, how long you train, an objective that can scale, and some normalization and conditioning so the numbers stay stable. If you get those right, you see these smooth, log-linear improvements.

Pre-training was the first place where that became really obvious. You put in more compute and more data, and the loss goes down in a very predictable way, and capabilities come along with it.

What we're seeing now with RL is, I think, the same phenomenon. People sometimes talk about it as if RL is a totally different paradigm, a new trick that replaces scaling. I don't really see it that way. When you train models with RL on tasks like math competitions, coding, or more open-ended agentic work, you see the same kind of log-linear relationship: performance goes up roughly with the log of how much you train. It's not that one replaced the other. It's more like we've found a second axis that behaves the way the first one did.

The two are also complementary. Pre-training gives you this enormously broad base: the model has absorbed a huge amount about the world, language, and how humans reason. RL takes that base and shapes it toward actually doing things, toward reaching goals, persisting through long chains of reasoning, and checking its own work. RL works better on a stronger pre-trained model, and pre-training on its own doesn't elicit everything the model is capable of.

One analogy I find useful, though like all analogies it's imperfect: pre-training is somewhere between evolution and human learning. It's not like a person reading a textbook. It's more like building up the priors and structure a human brain has before it learns anything specific. RL is closer to the learning you do on top of that, practicing a skill and getting feedback. Both matter, and both seem to scale.

There's a real question people raise about generalization. When you do RL on a specific set of tasks, does that transfer broadly, or do you just get narrow skills? Early pre-training had a similar story. When we trained on narrow datasets, models didn't generalize well. Once we trained on something as broad as a big crawl of the internet, generalization started to emerge. I suspect RL is going through the same transition. As the range of RL environments and tasks gets broader, you start getting more general capability rather than a collection of narrow tricks.

So my short answer is: I don't see a fundamental tension between them. It's the same scaling story continuing, and that's part of why I remain fairly confident the overall trend continues.

r001.rationale: The response says RL shows the same scaling phenomenon as pre-training.

r002.rationale: It says RL task performance rises roughly with the log of how much you train, conveying log-linear scaling with training duration.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the cleanest way to say it is that they're the same phenomenon showing up in two places. The thing we discovered with pre-training was that if you take a sufficiently general objective, a sufficiently flexible architecture, and you just keep scaling compute and data, the loss goes down in a very predictable way and capabilities come along with it. That was the surprising fact. It wasn't about next-token prediction per se. It was that large-scale learning on a broad distribution is smooth and predictable.

What happened with RL is that we found a second axis where the same thing is true. Pre-training is kind of free riding on the structure of human-generated data. It learns what humans already know. RL lets the model learn things that aren't in the data, because it's getting a signal from actually trying things and seeing what works. And it turns out that if you scale that, if you put more compute into the RL phase, you see curves that look a lot like the pre-training curves. They're a bit noisier, the environments matter more, but the basic shape is there.

So I don't think of RL as replacing pre-training. I think of pre-training as building the prior. It gives you a model that has a rich enough representation of the world that when you start doing RL, the model is exploring in a space that's already sensible. If you tried to do RL from scratch on these tasks, it wouldn't work. You'd never stumble into the right behaviors. And conversely, if you only did pre-training, you'd be capped at roughly imitating what's in the data.

The other thing I'd say is that the two scale differently in what they cost you. Pre-training is expensive in a very uniform way, you're buying general capability across everything. RL is more targeted. You get a lot of capability per unit of compute on the thing you're training for, and some of it generalizes, maybe more than people expected, but not all of it. So part of the art right now is figuring out the ratio. How much do you put into the base, how much into the RL phase, and which environments give you the most transfer. And I think the honest answer is we're still early in understanding that. Three years ago the RL part was a rounding error compared to pre-training. Now it's a meaningful fraction, and I'd expect it to keep growing.

But the underlying bet is the same one we've had the whole time. The thing that works is scale, applied to the right objective. We just found a second objective.

r001.rationale: The response says RL scaling shows curves that look a lot like pre-training curves and describes them as the same scaling phenomenon.

r002.rationale: It says RL performance improves as more compute is applied, but does not state that task performance scales log-linearly with training duration.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as two ways of spending compute to make the model better, but they’re operating on somewhat different things. In pre-training, the model learns from a very broad distribution of data. It acquires knowledge, representations, and a lot of capabilities that aren’t necessarily easy to elicit. With reinforcement learning, you’re giving it an opportunity to try things and get feedback about whether those things worked.

The interesting question is how independently those two processes scale. If you hold the pre-trained model fixed and do more reinforcement learning, how far can you go? And if you make the pre-trained model better, does that make every unit of reinforcement learning more effective? My intuition is that there’s a lot of complementarity. A better starting model can discover solutions that a weaker model would almost never stumble across, which gives the reinforcement-learning process something useful to reinforce.

But I wouldn’t assume that the scaling curves are identical. With pre-training, you have a fairly uniform objective over a huge amount of data. With reinforcement learning, a lot depends on the environments you construct, the tasks you give the model, and whether you can reliably measure success. You can get very good at the thing you’re rewarding without necessarily improving as much elsewhere.

So the way I’d frame it is that we’ve added another axis of scaling. That’s potentially very powerful, but we still have to understand the tradeoff: for a given compute budget, how much should go into building a stronger starting model, and how much should go into letting that model learn from experience?

r001.rationale: The candidate describes reinforcement learning as a separate scaling axis and says its scaling curves may differ from pre-training; it does not state that they exhibit the same kind of scaling behavior.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not state that reinforcement-learning task performance scales log-linearly with training duration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary, but I’d be careful about assuming they’re exactly the same phenomenon.

With pre-training, you have this very broad process of learning from enormous amounts of text and other data. You’re acquiring knowledge, representations, and some ability to reason. Reinforcement learning then gives you a way to take that starting point and improve it through trial and error: try to solve a problem, get feedback, and become more likely to use approaches that work.

The interesting question is how much reinforcement learning can discover beyond what’s already accessible to the pretrained model. There’s a spectrum between making the model reliably do something it could already occasionally do, and teaching it a substantially new capability. I don’t think we should assume that everything is at either end of that spectrum.

And the scaling constraints are different. In pre-training, a central question is how much useful data you have. In reinforcement learning, you also need tasks and feedback that actually distinguish good performance from bad performance. That’s relatively straightforward for some coding or math problems. It’s harder for a complicated real-world decision where you might not know whether you were right for six months.

So I’d think of them as interacting axes. A better pretrained model gives reinforcement learning a better starting point, and better reinforcement learning lets you get more out of that starting point. Seeing strong returns from one doesn’t establish that the other has stopped mattering.

r001.rationale: The response calls the methods complementary but cautions that they may not be the same phenomenon; it does not state that reinforcement learning exhibits the same scaling behavior as pre-training.

r002.rationale: The response discusses different scaling constraints but does not state that reinforcement-learning task performance scales log-linearly with training duration.
